gao-gaoreports-gao-05-395t:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, GAO-05-395T of March 9, 2005, gives early notes on the rise of pilot-free craft in war. Such craft have grown since the 1980s. They scout, watch, and strike with no crew at risk in the sky. As the Pentagon reshapes how it fights, the craft take a core role. Each service buys its own, in its own way.

GAO tells of wins in the field so far, drawn from work still in train. It names the new tests that crowd in, from air space to data flow. It asks if one grand plan and one watch arm steer the whole spend. Past craft lessons frame the plea.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-455t:
The first year of the Millennium Challenge Corporation is reviewed in testimony GAO-05-455T, given on April 26, 2005. Congress created the corporation in January 2004 to fund growth and cut deep poverty in poor countries. Aid flows mainly through compacts, which are deals with country governments. Congress gave the effort nearly $2.5 billion for fiscal years 2004 and 2005. GAO tracked how countries were chosen and how compacts were built.

The board named 17 countries as eligible for compacts across the two years. It used set measures of policy performance, mixed with its own judgment. GAO found that not all of the source data behind the measures was publicly available. Work on compacts, coordination with other aid bodies, and management systems was still young. GAO urged the corporation to build clear plans and time frames for accountability, internal control, and staffing. The testimony shows a new aid model taking shape.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-465t:
Oversight of Head Start grantees is questioned in testimony GAO-05-465T, presented on April 5, 2005. In fiscal year 2004 the program got $6.8 billion to serve 919,000 poor children through 1,680 grantees. Reports of money misuse at some programs raised doubts about federal oversight. GAO looked at how the Administration for Children and Families spots risk, checks its data, and fixes weak grantees.

The agency had no single system to pull its many checks into one view of risk. Site reviews did not always follow its own rules. Data sent in by grantees were not verified. Spending was matched to withdrawals only after all funds were gone. Staff often learned of trouble from calls by parents and teachers. More than half the grantees cited for money faults broke such rules again at their next review. Poor results rarely led to lost funding, and GAO urged a fuller approach to risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-485t:
Air traffic modernization under the new Air Traffic Organization is weighed in testimony GAO-05-485T, given on April 14, 2005. The Federal Aviation Administration has tried for more than two decades to update its control systems. Projects kept missing cost, schedule, and performance goals. The work has been on GAO's high-risk list since 1995. The new organization runs the system and plans upgrades on a rolling 10-year view.

The organization had taken some sound steps, GAO said. It brought users in early and cut big projects that missed their goals. Its handling of technology work had improved. But it did not use the knowledge-based buying method that top buyers follow. A process model for software work was used in some projects but not required in all. Ahead lay a 25 percent rise in air traffic over 10 years and the hiring of thousands of new controllers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-605t:
Improper payments across the government are the subject of this testimony, GAO-05-605T of July 12, 2005. The Improper Payments Information Act of 2002 made agencies find programs prone to error, estimate the sums, and report their fixes each year. Fiscal year 2004 was the first year of that duty governmentwide. GAO reviewed the annual reports of 29 large agencies for that year.

Seventeen agencies reported over $45 billion in improper payments across 41 programs. That was up almost $10 billion, or 27 percent, from fiscal 2003. Much of the rise came from a changed method in Medicare. Some agencies still had not assessed every program or built estimates, so the true size stayed unknown. Twelve programs with $248.7 billion in outlays had no figures at all.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-625t:
The Millennium Challenge Corporation's first year is tracked in GAO-05-625T, testimony dated April 27, 2005. Set up in January 2004, the agency gives large grants to poor nations that govern well, judged by set measures. Congress gave it nearly $2.5 billion for fiscal 2004 and 2005; $3 billion more was sought for 2006. Its board picked 17 countries as fit for compacts, using the measures plus judgment.

GAO tracked country picks, compact talks, and links with other aid bodies. It told the agency's chief to finish plans for firm-wide controls, staffing, and answerability, with dates. Growth was real, but the frame lagged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-655t:
Fairness in veterans' disability rulings is revisited in GAO testimony GAO-05-655T (May 5, 2005). It updates a 2002 study of the Board of Veterans' Appeals. The board fixed how it samples rulings for quality checks, so late-year cases now count. It also stopped counting harmless errors in its accuracy rate. One formula fix remains undone, though GAO says it would barely move the rate.

The wider worry stands: average payments per veteran vary sharply by state, and the department still has no steady way to test whether like cases get like rulings. Studies by its inspector general and benefits arm are under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-675t:
Gasoline price spikes are explained in GAO testimony GAO-05-675T of May 9, 2005. The average price hit $2.20 a gallon, up 23 percent in a year; California paid $2.57, the nation's most. Households were set to spend about $350 more on fuel in 2005 than in 2004. Crude oil drives the pump price: the benchmark crude rose almost $20 a barrel, near 60 percent, since January 2004. World demand growth, Gulf tensions, and OPEC restraint pushed it up.

Refinery capacity has lagged demand at home. California's cleaner-burning blend sets its market apart and adds cost. Forecasts split between lasting highs and a fall.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-755t:
Flight delays are the topic of testimony GAO-05-755T, presented May 26, 2005. One in five flights ran late in 2004. New York and Chicago airports drove much of the problem. Air travel was rising again after a sharp drop. Passengers grew from 642 million in 2003 to 688 million in 2004. GAO listed live fixes, hard blocks, and other options.

GAO found many fixes under way. A federal plan from February 2005 aims at 35 of the busiest airports over 10 years. Seven new runways opened in 6 years, and seven more were due by the end of 2008. Caps limit flights at the worst airports in peak hours. Funding is the chief block, GAO said. Crowded sites also have little room to grow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-795t:
Housing help for the elderly is surveyed in testimony GAO-05-795T, presented June 16, 2005. The elderly share of the population is set to grow from about 12 percent in 2002 to 20 percent by 2030. Over one-third of elderly tenants in aided housing need help with daily tasks. GAO listed which aid programs must supply support services. It named other programs and partners that can help.

GAO reviewed 23 housing programs. Only 4 require owners to make services like meals or rides available. Three are housing department programs, and one is a rural loan program. Four more housing programs can be used to link elderly tenants to services. Health programs and private partners can also fill gaps. The testimony maps where help is required and where it is only possible.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-825t:
Rehab hospital classes under Medicare are discussed in testimony GAO-05-825T, delivered June 16, 2005. A rule sorts these hospitals by case mix. At least 75 percent of patients must need intense rehab for 1 of 13 listed conditions. Passing the test brings a higher pay rate. So the class call matters a lot. The testimony rests on an April 2005 GAO report on the rule.

For that report, GAO studied data on all Medicare patients admitted to such hospitals in fiscal year 2003. It spoke with medical directors. It also had a medical body convene experts on the list of conditions. The shared verdict gives the testimony its title. The criteria need to be more specific. Only then can hospitals be classed correctly and paid at the right level.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-835t:
An earlier take on the same airline strain is testimony GAO-05-835T, delivered June 22, 2005. Two of the largest U.S. airlines had entered bankruptcy. Their ended pension plans passed a $9.6 billion gap to the federal insurer. Members lost $5.2 billion in benefits. Debate raged over whether bankruptcy gives failed carriers an unfair edge. GAO gave early views on the legacy carriers, on bankruptcy effects, and on pension fallout.

GAO found the legacy carriers still cannot cut costs to rival levels. They have lost $28 billion since 2001. Bankruptcy is common in the field: 160 filings since 1978. GAO saw no clear proof that bankrupt carriers harm rivals. But pension members and the insurer do get hurt. The remaining legacy carriers face over $60 billion in fixed duties over the next 4 years. Pension payments make up $10.4 billion of that.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-845t:
The shift to Internet protocol version 6 is explained in testimony GAO-05-845T, presented June 29, 2005. The current protocol's address pool may not fit the growing mass of users and devices. The new version uses 128-bit addresses in place of 32-bit ones. That opens a vastly larger address space. GAO drew on its recent study of agency planning for the shift.

GAO said agencies must plan now, since new gear already carries the protocol. Key steps include taking stock, weighing risks, and building a business case. Costs and timelines must be set, and security risks managed. The Defense Department has made real progress on these fronts. Most other big agencies, GAO found, have not yet begun key planning work. GAO urged the budget office to direct agencies to start.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-855t:
Federal help against Medicaid fraud is measured in testimony GAO-05-855T, presented June 28, 2005. The program covered nearly 54 million people in fiscal year 2003. Benefit payments came to roughly $261 billion. The federal share was about $153 billion. States hold the front line against fraud. The federal Medicaid agency backs and oversees their work.

GAO's focus is the level of resources that federal backing gets. Prior GAO work found the agency had helpful initiatives. But the dollars and staff assigned looked small next to the federal money at risk. The testimony updates that resource picture. It then weighs what limited commitment means for guarding program funds. The title gives the verdict: the agency's commitment to helping states is limited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1005t:
Home brokerage rivalry returns in testimony GAO-06-1005T, presented July 25, 2006. Consumers paid an estimated $65.7 billion in brokerage fees in 2005. Rates stay much the same across markets and effort. Some economists doubt how hard brokers compete on price. Internet brokers still hold a small market share. The testimony rests on an August 2005 GAO report.

GAO discusses what shapes price competition in the field. It then covers the state of Internet brokerage and what blocks its growth. The earlier report found rivalry runs more on service and reputation than on fees. Shared listing services and some state rules play a part in that pattern. This testimony brings that case to a new hearing, updated with the 2005 fee total.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1125t:
Senior executive performance management is the topic of GAO-06-1125T, testimony given on September 26, 2006. In November 2003 Congress scrapped set yearly pay raises for senior executives. The new system ties pay to results, for both the person and the agency. Agencies whose systems win certification from the Office of Personnel Management, with budget office agreement, may pay top performers above old caps. GAO reviewed the rules, the certification path, and how the system is watched.

Past GAO work found that executive reviews often failed to link personal goals to agency results. The testimony explains how certification tests whether an agency's system makes that link. It reports agency views of the process and how many agencies had won certification so far. It also covers the personnel office's duty to monitor the system over time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-135t:
Foreign purchases of U.S. firms and the security review behind them are covered in GAO-06-135T, testimony from October 2005. The 1988 Exon-Florio law lets the President block foreign deals that threaten national security. The President has used that power only once. An interagency committee runs the reviews, weighing security risks against open investment policy. GAO reported flaws in that process in September 2002. This statement reports a deeper look.

GAO suggested that Congress sharpen the law's list of harm factors. Members disagree on what counts as a security threat. GAO also urged one 75-day review period in place of split review and investigation stages. Firms now often withdraw and refile deals to gain time; 18 deals had done so since 1997. That tactic can leave live risks unguarded. GAO proposed interim safeguards and set refile deadlines. It also sought broader reporting to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-175t:
Illegal prescription drug imports by mail are targeted in GAO-06-175T, testimony presented on December 13, 2005. Customs and Border Protection and the Food and Drug Administration inspect mail and carrier sites for banned drugs. Other agencies join them at those hubs. GAO summed up its report on the volume and safety of these drugs. It covered inspection methods, the forces that limit enforcement, and how well agencies coordinate.

Data on these imports is thin. Neither agency tracks volume or safety in a systematic way. What little is known suggests real risk to buyers who order from abroad. GAO urged the border agency and its task force partners to build a shared strategic framework. It also urged the health department to test a change in how buyers are told about seized drugs. Most agencies backed the framework idea. The Postal Service asked that world postal duties be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-225t:
Budget candor at the veterans benefits agency is the theme of GAO-06-225T, testimony presented on November 3, 2005. The Veterans Benefits Administration asked Congress for fewer claims staff in fiscal year 2005. At the same time it faced a growing workload. In November 2004 GAO reported that the agency's budget case could have been clearer. This statement shares those findings with a House panel.

The agency never clearly said how its plans would offset the cuts, GAO found. It gave no firm account of the productivity gains it counted on. It claimed claims grow more complex but did not project that growth or its cost. GAO urged fuller detail on each point in future budget cases. The agency agreed to add such detail in the fiscal year 2007 and 2008 rounds. Its fiscal year 2006 case already set more reachable goals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-235t:
Disaster contracting after two Gulf hurricanes is previewed in GAO-06-235T, testimony dated November 2, 2005. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita wrecked parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Texas. The storms raised hard doubts about how well the government responds. Federal disaster work leans more each year on private contractors. Yet buying offices at several agencies sit on GAO's high-risk list. GAO outlined its own role in judging the contract work. It shared its review plans and its first findings on how the response went.

Speed in a crisis invites waste and fraud. No-bid deals and loose oversight marked past disaster buys. GAO said it would test how agencies and their firms prepared and performed. Early lessons would shape the reviews to come. The testimony sets a marker: relief must move fast and still answer for its cost.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-245t:
In testimony dated November 17, 2005, GAO returned to the sale of costly financial products to service members. A small set of firms, accused of deceptive pitches, target troops with deals that shrink what buyers get. One product pairs life insurance with a savings pot. If payments stop and no refund is claimed, the savings get eaten to keep the policy alive. Most troops leave service in a few years, so most savers likely built nothing.

A second product, the mutual fund contractual plan, has nearly vanished from civilian sales. Its front-loaded charges punish anyone who stops paying early, as many troops do. The largest seller has already been sanctioned for misleading sales material. A core failure sits with the Defense Department: base staff rarely shared complaints with regulators. Without complaints, watchdogs could not see the pattern early.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-335t:
A flood insurance program drowned by one storm season is the topic of GAO-06-335T, testimony presented January 25, 2006. The National Flood Insurance Program dates to 1968. The emergency agency runs it from inside Homeland Security. The 2005 hurricanes brought a record flood of claims. Katrina, Rita, and Wilma alone may cost about $23 billion. That tops every claim paid in the program's prior history. GAO drew on past and current work for this statement.

The testimony covers the program's shaky finances. It weighs the drag of homes that flood again and again. It reviews ideas to draw more owners into coverage. It checks the fate of earlier GAO advice. The agency still owes fixes ordered by a 2004 reform law, GAO noted. Claim handbooks, an appeals path, and agent training remain due. The statement frames a program built for ordinary years facing a catastrophic one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-465t:
The costliest census in U.S. history was being planned while hurricanes displaced whole cities. Delivered March 1, 2006, testimony GAO-06-465T reports on planning for the 2010 Census. The Census Bureau put the cost at about $11.3 billion. That would top all prior censuses, even after adjusting for inflation. Careful planning is key to a sound count, GAO notes.

GAO reports progress in planning and testing work. It weighs challenges that Hurricanes Katrina and Rita may pose for later census work. It also stresses planning for events that could badly disrupt the count. Planning and testing are making progress, GAO said. Readers get an early status report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-555t:
This statement carries a March plant security report into testimony form. Testimony GAO-06-555T, given April 4, 2006, is based on GAO-06-388 on nuclear power plant security. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission revised its design basis threat in April 2003. That standard defines the attackers plants must be ready to repel. The commission also rebuilt its force-on-force testing, which uses mock attacks. Plants are possible terror targets because a breach could release radioactive material.

GAO covers how the commission built the 2003 threat standard. It reports actions plants took to upgrade security. It reviews efforts to strengthen the mock attack tests. Plants have upgraded security, GAO said. The threat process still needs improvement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-585t:
More money for weapons has not bought more stability, GAO told Congress. GAO's GAO-06-585T testimony, delivered April 5, 2006, seeks better results from weapon system investments. In five years, the Defense Department doubled planned investment in weapons. Outcomes did not improve with the money. Programs keep facing cost overruns, missed deadlines, and performance shortfalls. Buying power for the acquisition dollar has not grown.

GAO names three steps for a better foundation. First, a department-wide strategy that ranks programs by realistic threat needs. Second, enforcing current policy so new programs can be executed. Third, clear accountability for results. Past GAO reports made similar recommendations, the statement notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-605t:
Small business loan programs run by the Small Business Administration are the subject of this GAO testimony, GAO-06-605T, released on April 6, 2006. SBA backs loans through its 7(a) program, where private lenders make loans that SBA guarantees. Its disaster office also lends directly to homes and firms hurt by disasters. The testimony draws on GAO reports issued since 1998.

GAO told the Senate panel that SBA had built a lender oversight office in 1999, after having almost no oversight in the mid-1990s. The agency had also improved its technology, staffing, and loan reporting work. Yet GAO said weak spots remained in how SBA ran its loan and disaster aid work. Readers get a clear scorecard of gains made and risks still open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-615t:
Tax season results and the tax agency budget are reviewed in GAO testimony GAO-06-615T, dated April 6, 2006. The Internal Revenue Service serves tens of millions of taxpayers who expect fast refunds and correct answers. Its budget request for fiscal year 2007 shows how it planned to serve taxpayers and enforce tax law. GAO noted that the tax gap, what taxpayers owe but do not pay on time, was estimated at $345 billion for 2001.

GAO assessed early results from the 2006 filing season and compared them with past years. GAO also weighed whether the budget request would help the agency meet its long-term goals. Those goals include raising tax compliance and cutting public tolerance for cheating. The testimony gives a clear snapshot of agency performance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-665t:
Construction of the Capitol Visitor Center is updated in GAO-06-665T, testimony presented on April 27, 2006. The underground center was being built to receive tourists and tighten security at the Capitol. The Architect of the Capitol still proposed the same opening dates given at a March 15 hearing. The base project would open in April 2007, and House and Senate expansion spaces in May 2007.

GAO told the panel that building work had moved forward since March. Even so, GAO continued to doubt the proposed opening dates. The dates did not leave enough time to finish several critical activities, such as testing systems and moving in. GAO warned that holding to the dates raised cost and schedule risk for the project.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-715t:
Medicare's own mailings on the new drug benefit are assessed in GAO-06-715T, testimony GAO gave on May 4, 2006. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services had to explain Part D to millions of seniors in a short time. It produced a large volume of material and shared it through many channels. GAO reviewed six of its written documents in detail. GAO also weighed how well the material served beneficiaries and their advisers.

GAO credited the agency with building so much information so quickly. But GAO said the quality of the communications could be improved. Some documents were dense, unclear, or hard to compare across plans. Seniors risked picking a plan that did not fit their drug needs. GAO pressed for plainer, more useful guidance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-755t:
Charities that owe taxes are exposed in GAO-06-755T, testimony presented on May 25, 2006. The Combined Federal Campaign is the federal workplace giving drive, run by the Office of Personnel Management. It gave more than 22,000 charities access to federal donors. The 2005 campaign collected more than $250 million in donations. Donor trust depends on charities handling gifts with care.

GAO found that more than 1,280 campaign charities had federal tax debts totaling $35.6 million. Unpaid payroll taxes made up almost 80 percent of the debt. GAO warned that the true amount owed was understated in its count. Some charities with tax debts had also received substantial federal funds. The testimony raised sharp questions about screening charities that solicit federal workers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-855t:
Linking travel modes into one system is the theme of GAO-06-855T, testimony GAO gave on June 15, 2006. Intermodal transport joins trains, trucks, ships, planes, and buses into smooth trips for people and freight. Rising travel and freight volume have clogged the nation's networks. Experts expect the growth to continue. GAO set out the challenges to building better intermodal connections, and strategies that might help.

GAO found that financing and planning hurdles shape most intermodal choices. A core problem is the lack of clear national goals and funding programs for such projects. Federal money is often tied to a single mode, so joint projects struggle to qualify. That bias favors highways or rail alone over combined terminals and links. GAO offered strategies to give intermodal work a fairer place in investment plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-865t:
Private guards in Iraq are the subject of GAO-06-865T, testimony presented on June 13, 2006. Thousands of armed contractors protect convoys, sites, and officials in the war zone. GAO was asked how far coordination between the military and these firms had improved since its 2005 report. GAO also checked background screening of guard employees. A third question asked whether United States or global standards govern such providers.

GAO found progress mixed with open gaps. Coordination had improved in some ways since 2005. But screening had real limits, including the reach of the Defense Department's biometric checks in Iraq. GAO also found no established standards to guide contractors in hiring and vetting staff. Actions were still needed, GAO said, to improve how private security providers are used. The testimony weighs a wartime necessity against its risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-875t:
Placing baggage scanners in airports is planned in GAO-06-875T, testimony GAO gave on June 29, 2006. The Transportation Security Administration screens checked bags with two kinds of gear. Large detection systems scan bags with X-rays, while trace systems swab bags for explosive residue. The agency views the large scanners as the stronger tool. Where they sit in an airport shapes cost, speed, and safety. GAO updated Congress on the deployment plans.

GAO said the agency had strengthened its efforts to plan the best placement of the systems. Stand-alone scanners had created operational problems at some airports. In-line systems, built into baggage belts, offer gains in efficiency, safety, and security. The agency had begun systematic planning for those layouts. Funding uncertainties, though, still cloud the schedule. Congress holds the purse for the costly retrofits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-885t:
War costs since 2001 are tracked in GAO testimony GAO-06-885T, dated July 18, 2006, on the Global War on Terrorism. Work in Iraq and Afghanistan forms a key part of that effort. It spans combat, civil aid, rebuilding, and training local forces.

GAO set out funds Congress had given the Defense Department and other agencies for these operations. It then weighed the costs agencies reported, and how sound those cost figures were. Last, it raised the hard task of gauging future U.S. costs. The testimony helps readers see both the sums spent and the doubt around long-term pledges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-895t:
Worksite checks and proof of work rights are the focus of GAO testimony GAO-06-895T, dated June 19, 2006. Jobs draw many people to enter the United States without legal status. The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 set a check process and fines for firms that break it.

The testimony rests on GAO's August 2005 report. GAO set out flaws in the check process as it then stood. It also weighed the aims, staff, and funds of Immigration and Customs Enforcement for worksite action. GAO pressed for a set time frame to fix the rules. Readers see why weak checks blunt enforcement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-905t:
Shared health data between the Veterans Affairs and Defense departments is one of two big tech efforts in GAO testimony GAO-06-905T, dated June 22, 2006. Shared records affect care for active troops and veterans alike. The second effort is VETSNET, a new system for paying veterans' benefits.

GAO tracked near-term steps to swap data through current systems. It also tracked the longer plan to link both departments' new health systems. For VETSNET, it checked build progress against past GAO advice. The testimony shows two large federal tech builds, and the strain of keeping care and benefits moving while they change.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-915t:
Plans for a next era air traffic system are set out in GAO testimony GAO-06-915T, dated July 25, 2006. The current system grows less fit and more dated each year. In 2003 Congress set up a joint planning office, housed at the Federal Aviation Administration, to plan the shift with seven partner agencies.

GAO shared early results from work still in progress. It told where planning stood for the new system. It named the chief hurdles for the planning office. It also named hurdles for the aviation agency, which must change the system while still running daily flights. The testimony frames a long, joint build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1025t:
Public housing renewal under HOPE VI is summed up in GAO testimony GAO-07-1025T, dated June 20, 2007. Since fiscal year 1992 the Department of Housing and Urban Development has given over $6 billion in HOPE VI grants. The grants rebuild badly worn public housing and aid the people who live there.

Housing bodies were urged to draw other funds to match the grants. GAO drew on three reports from November 2002 to November 2003. It set out how projects are funded, and how much extra money they drew. It weighed federal watch over the program. It traced effects on residents and nearby streets, plus agency replies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1075t:
Guard plans for key national systems are done, and joint councils are taking shape, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1075T, dated July 12, 2007. About 85 percent of key infrastructure is in private hands. Public and private players must thus guard it together. Hurricane Katrina showed how wide the threats run.

The Homeland Security Department led a national guard plan, with councils for 17 sectors. GAO told how far sector plans meet the set terms. It gave members' views on the plans' worth, and on the department's review. It named what helps councils form and last, and what blocks them. The work rests on GAO's July 2007 report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1095t:
Energy trading and its watch are given early GAO views in testimony GAO-07-1095T, dated July 12, 2007. Prices for crude oil, heating oil, gasoline, and natural gas had risen sharply since 2002. Some blame supply and demand alone. Others say futures trading played a part.

GAO shared early findings on trends in futures and physical energy markets. It weighed how those trends bear on prices. It set out the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's power to rule and enforce in these markets. The work mined exchange trading data, trader reports, studies, and talks with market players, experts, and officials. The word early matters: these are first views.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1115t:
A Pacific island state's aid pact is tracked in GAO testimony GAO-07-1115T, dated July 24, 2007. From 1987 through 2003 the United States gave over $2 billion to Micronesia and the Marshall Islands under a Compact of Free Association. About $579 million of that went to the Marshall Islands.

A renewed pact in 2003 adds 20 years of aid, about $1.5 billion from 2004 through 2023. Grants shrink each year, while trust fund payments grow. The aim is budget self-reliance when grants end in 2023. GAO weighed the islands' economic outlook and pact work since 2005. Steps have moved ahead, GAO said, but long-term aims face hard tests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1125t:
Marshall Islands aid gets a second GAO airing in testimony GAO-07-1125T, dated July 25, 2007, a day after a mate statement on the same pact. In 2003 the United States renewed aid under an amended Compact of Free Association. From 2004 to 2023 it will give an estimated $1.5 billion.

Grants fall each year, while trust fund sums rise. The fund should yield income when grants end. Aid targets six sectors, toward growth and budget self-reliance. GAO weighed the islands' outlook, pact work toward long goals, and likely fund earnings. It rests on five past reports. The Interior Department agreed with past GAO advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1135t:
Export controls leak and lag, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1135T, dated July 26, 2007. The system must keep arms and dual-use tech from wrong hands, while letting lawful trade flow. New threats and a world market have made that balance harder. The State Department rules arms exports. The Commerce Department rules dual-use goods.

GAO has long reported flaws in this system, with advice still not in place. The statement picks three fields: flaws that open the system to misuse, slow license work, and a lack of tests by both departments on how well their controls work. Flaws and waste, the title states, blunt the system's guard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1235t:
Civilian Defense Department workers deploy to war zones beside the troops they support. GAO discussed their medical coverage and pay in testimony GAO-07-1235T, issued September 18, 2007. The statement draws on GAO's September 2006 report on the topic. GAO reviewed more than 3,400 deployment records at eight locations. It also checked workers' compensation claims and compared civilian and military benefits.

GAO found that the department had health protection and medical treatment policies in place. But it had no quality assurance step to make sure units followed them. Some units lacked records showing required health checks before deployment. Only 52 of 3,771 records missed proof of a pre-deployment health assessment. GAO also found gaps in central data on who had deployed. A new policy in February 2007 aimed to fix that tracking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1245t:
Freight rail rates have split shippers ever since Congress deregulated the industry in 1980. GAO updated Congress on rates and competition in GAO-07-1245T on September 25, 2007. The testimony builds on GAO reports from October 2006 and August 2007. It tracks industry change since the Staggers Rail Act of 1980. It also covers shippers with no real transport alternatives, called captive shippers.

GAO reported that rail finances had improved and most rates had fallen since 1985. But rates began rising in 2001. In 2005, they jumped 9 percent over the prior year. Railroads had also shifted costs onto shippers over 20 years. Revenue classed as miscellaneous, including fuel surcharges, grew ten-fold from 2000 to 2005. It rose from about $141 million to over $1.7 billion. GAO closed with the Surface Transportation Board's steps on its advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1255t:
After Hurricane Katrina, Congress wanted to know whether small firms shared in the recovery contracts. GAO answered with observations in GAO-07-1255T, dated September 26, 2007. The testimony pulls from GAO's March 2007 report on Katrina contracting. Four agencies awarded about $11 billion directly for Katrina projects. GAO also reviewed how agencies and the Small Business Administration speak up for small firms.

Small businesses received 28 percent of those direct contract dollars, GAO found. Homeland Security gave small firms the most money, about $1.6 billion. The General Services Administration gave the highest share, 72 percent of about $658 million. GAO also found big holes in the official contracting data. For 70 percent or more of the dollars at two agencies, records did not show whether subcontracting plans were required. That gap weakens checks on how much work flows to small subcontractors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1265t:
About 196,000 veterans were homeless in 2006, and shelter beds fell short of the need. GAO discussed one aid program in GAO-07-1265T, presented September 27, 2007. The Grant and Per Diem program funds transitional housing run by local providers. The testimony sums up GAO's September 2006 report on the program. A House subcommittee on veterans' health asked for the briefing.

The program had quadrupled its bed capacity since 2000, GAO reported. It reached about 8,200 beds, with more growth planned. Providers faced a changing population, with more women and veterans with children. GAO found that providers and local liaisons mostly worked well together. But some providers misunderstood basic program rules. A few wrongly thought veterans had to qualify for VA health care to take part. Others missed that the three-stay lifetime limit could be waived.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-225t:
Bombings in London and Mumbai showed how open passenger trains are to attack. GAO updated Congress on rail security in testimony GAO-07-225T on January 18, 2007. The statement rests on GAO's September 2005 report plus fresh program updates. It covers how the homeland security department sizes up rail risks. It reviews federal steps to harden rail systems. It also lists practices used by rail operators at home and abroad.

Federal risk work was still unfinished, GAO said. The transport security agency had no method yet for ranking rail risks. Without one, it cannot aim scarce funds at the biggest gains. Operators on both sides of the ocean used like measures, GAO found. Twenty-nine of 32 U.S. operators had camera systems in place. All ruled out airport-style screening for daily crowds. Foreign systems used covert testing and random screening, which U.S. operators did not.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-385t:
GAO used this testimony to show Congress how it audits the Iraq war effort. The statement, GAO-07-385T of January 18, 2007, covers scope and method. GAO has issued 67 Iraq reports and testimonies since 2003. Its teams briefed the Iraq Study Group in June 2006. Much source material is classified. GAO works to publish findings in open form. The statement also lists headline results from the body of work.

Security in Iraq worsened even as Iraqi forces grew, GAO reports. Readiness strains hit U.S. units at home and abroad. Gear reset programs are under way in both ground services. Contracting with unclear terms added cost and risk. The national strategy met only part of GAO's effectiveness tests. An international peer team gave GAO's quality system a clean opinion in April 2005. It was only the second such rating ever granted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-395t: Preparing for the next disaster was the 2007 theme, and GAO's briefing surveys Homeland Security's readiness and response posture. The testimony takes the full measure of the effort. The findings warn that the nation was better at planning the response than funding it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-525t: Iraq was a fraudster's paradise in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the conditions practically invited waste and abuse of the rebuild money. The testimony paints the free-for-all in stark terms. The findings warn that billions flowed exactly where the watchdogs could not follow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-545t: Transportation's troubles got a scorecard in 2007, and GAO's briefing lays out the challenges facing Congress and the department. The testimony inventories the gridlock in detail. The findings warn that the nation's arteries were clogging faster than the fixes. The roads were not waiting for Washington.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-575t: The Coast Guard's big cutter program was troubled in 2007, and GAO's briefing reviews the Deepwater management fixes and the operational strains. The testimony takes stock. The findings warn that the fleet of the future needed steadier hands on the helm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-595t: Life after the space shuttle was the question in 2007 — GAO's briefing examines the handoff to the next human spaceflight systems. The testimony probes the coming gap in detail. The findings warn that the ride to orbit had no guaranteed successor.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-615t: The federal mortgage insurer was walking a tightrope in 2007, and GAO's briefing says its ability to manage risks would decide its financial fate. The testimony previews the danger. The findings warn that the housing backstop was only as strong as its risk controls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-625t: The FAA's money plumbing was being reworked in 2007, and GAO's briefing eyes the selected changes to the agency's funding structure. The testimony previews the stakes for travelers everywhere. The findings ask the blunt question: who would pay for the skies of tomorrow?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-635t: The war on wasteful payments ground on in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the agencies kept working the improper-payment and recovery-audit rules. The testimony tracks the grind in detail. The findings' refrain: count the errors, chase the dollars, and repeat.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-685t: The new postal law was a toolbox in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the reform gave the mail service real ways to face its challenges. The testimony inventories the opportunities one by one. The findings' question lingers: would the tools get used, or just gather dust?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-725t: The Smithsonian's roofs were leaking money in 2007 — GAO's briefing says funding the upkeep of the properties stayed a real challenge. The testimony tours the long list of deferred repairs. The findings' plea: the nation's attic should not crumble away from neglect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-755t: April brought no relief for the Capitol's basement project in 2007 — GAO's briefing logs the Visitor Center's latest time overruns and costs. The testimony's refrain stayed grim quarter after quarter. The findings kept the congressional microscope fixed firmly on Congress's own money pit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-775t: Veterans' college aid was tangled in red tape in 2007 — GAO's briefing says overlapping approval chores needed real trimming. The testimony targets the duplication in detail. The findings argue that the benefit should not require a second education just to claim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-785t: The food-safety system earned the high-risk label in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the designation could spotlight the government's fragmented watch. The testimony makes the case for the black mark. The findings argue that dinner should not be a gamble.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-795t: Selling America abroad was getting more professional in 2007 — GAO's briefing says public-diplomacy planning had improved, but execution still stumbled badly. The testimony balances credit with sharp critique. The findings argue that the message matters less than how it gets delivered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-835t: The next big storm was a when-not-if in 2007 — GAO's briefing sizes up DHS and FEMA's readiness for the catastrophic one. The testimony measures promises against machinery. The findings' unease is plain: the nation was better warned than prepared.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-855t: Coal miners were still dying preventable deaths in 2007 — GAO's briefing says better watch by the mine agency and its federal partners could save them. The testimony demands sharper oversight underground. The findings' moral is old as mining: the seam does not forgive slack safety.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-895t: The government's attics and warehouses stayed a high-risk mess in 2007 — GAO's briefing updates Congress on the federal property sprawl. The testimony tracks the vacant, costly, and crumbling holdings. The findings' refrain: the nation's landlord still did not know what it owned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-905t: American food aid was tripping over itself in 2007 — GAO's briefing says tangled rules sapped the efficiency of the hunger fight abroad. The testimony lists the snags slowing the grain. The findings ask an uncomfortable question: did the aid feed the hungry, or just the bureaucracy?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-935t: Sensitive data stayed at risk in 2007 despite the progress reports — GAO's briefing says agencies claimed gains while the crown jewels stayed exposed. The testimony punctures the happy talk with hard facts. The findings' refrain: reported progress is not the same as protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-985t: VA bosses were getting bonuses in 2007 — GAO's briefing examines the payouts to senior executives at the veterans agency and what they rewarded. The testimony asks what the bonuses actually bought for veterans. The findings probe whether the rewards matched the results, or just the rank.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-995t: States were fumbling the trade-aid handoff in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the adjustment program needed changes so states could actually deliver the help. The testimony diagnoses the delivery gap in detail. The findings argue that benefits on paper are not benefits in hand.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-115t: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that a new EPA rule could dim the public's view of toxic releases — the data that lets neighborhoods see what local plants puff out. Less public data hits poor and minority blocks hardest, GAO argued, since they already breathe the worst air. The briefing defends the right to know as an environmental justice issue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-135t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that the State Department's own watchdog was working with one hand tied. Short funds, thin access, and shaky standing kept the inspector general from fully grading U.S. diplomacy and aid. The briefing lays out the structural kinks — and argues that a watchdog that cannot bite is just a pet.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-215t: GAO gave Congress a split verdict on drug aid to Mexico in 2007: U.S. help had boosted the drug war south of the border, yet the northbound flow barely budged. The briefing captures the grind of a partnership winning skirmishes while losing the larger fight — and it fed a hard debate over whether the aid money was buying real results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-225t: A striking 2007 Government Accountability Office report: undercover tests exposed serious vulnerabilities in the Transportation Department's drug-testing program for safety-sensitive workers. Investigators found ways to cheat the tests used for truck drivers, pilots, and others whose jobs affect public safety. The report describes the exploits and demands fixes to a testing regime millions of workers depend on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-255t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony confronts long-standing concerns about how states finance their share of Medicaid. Some states used arrangements that shifted costs to the federal government in ways Congress never intended. GAO argues these schemes — documented over many years — support the need for stronger federal oversight of the joint state-federal health program's financing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-275t: Testimony from 2007 in which the Government Accountability Office turns the spotlight on itself: the diversity of its own Senior Executive Service. As the government's audit agency, GAO felt it should model the workforce diversity it often asks agencies to improve. The testimony reviews its recruitment, promotion, and mentoring efforts, and reports on how diverse its top leadership ranks had become.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-285t: In 2007 GAO briefed Congress on the hunt for nuclear terror plots: how ready were federal teams to spot and stop a smuggled bomb, and how safe were the posts that would lead the reply? The verdict was blunt — work remained. The report lists the weak spots in the nation's shield against the worst kind of attack.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-95t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony makes the case that 401(k) participants and plan sponsors need better information on fees.
